clinicalPearls: A rare inherited genodermatosis characterised by lifelong abnormal susceptibility to specific beta-genus human papillomaviruses, most often caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TMC6 (EVER1) or TMC8 (EVER2).
Presents in childhood with widespread flat wart-like papules together with reddish-brown or hypopigmented pityriasis versicolor-like macules on the face, neck, trunk and limbs.
The characteristic oncogenic beta-HPV types, notably HPV5 and HPV8, confer a high lifetime risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, especially at sun-exposed sites.
Malignant transformation typically emerges from the third to fourth decades, driven by combined viral and ultraviolet damage.
Strict lifelong photoprotection is central to reducing the risk of malignant transformation.
An acquired EV-like phenotype occurs with T-cell immunodeficiency, such as HIV infection, transplantation immunosuppression or GATA2 deficiency, and must be distinguished from the inherited disease.
Lesions are typically refractory and recurrent, so the goal is surveillance and early treatment of malignancy rather than cure.
Consanguinity and affected siblings support the usual autosomal recessive inheritance.
reference.pathophysiology: Classic epidermodysplasia verruciformis results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in TMC6 (EVER1) or TMC8 (EVER2) on chromosome 17q25, which encode transmembrane proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum that form a complex with the zinc transporter ZnT-1 and help regulate intracellular zinc homeostasis in keratinocytes. Their loss produces a selective intrinsic keratinocyte susceptibility to beta-papillomaviruses, permitting unchecked cutaneous replication of otherwise commensal beta-HPV types. Persistent infection with oncogenic types such as HPV5 and HPV8, acting together with ultraviolet-induced DNA damage, drives keratinocyte transformation and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Because the defect is largely confined to cutaneous immunity against these viruses, affected individuals are otherwise generally not broadly immunodeficient, in contrast to acquired EV where a systemic T-cell defect underlies the phenotype. Rarer forms have been linked to other genes affecting keratinocyte antiviral immunity, such as CIB1.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired epidermodysplasia verruciformis (HIV infection, iatrogenic immunosuppression, GATA2 or other T-cell immunodeficiencies)
Extensive common or plane warts (verruca plana) without the underlying genodermatosis
Pityriasis versicolor, which the macular lesions closely mimic
Tinea corporis and other superficial dermatoses
Seborrhoeic and actinic keratoses in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing the characteristic enlarged keratinocytes with blue-grey cytoplasm (EV cells)
HPV typing by PCR from lesional skin, seeking beta-HPV types, especially HPV5 and HPV8
Molecular genetic testing of TMC6 and TMC8 and related genes
Assessment for immunodeficiency to distinguish acquired EV, including HIV testing and lymphocyte subsets
Dermoscopy and regular total-body skin surveillance
Biopsy of any changing, indurated or ulcerated lesion to detect squamous cell carcinoma
redFlags: A lesion becoming indurated, ulcerated, painful or rapidly enlarging, suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
New lesions concentrated on sun-exposed skin
Onset of an EV-like eruption in an adult, prompting a search for acquired immunodeficiency
Regional lymphadenopathy suggesting metastatic cutaneous malignancy
reference.prognosis: Skin lesions persist lifelong; the major determinant of outcome is cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, which is often multiple and can be locally aggressive, so prognosis depends on rigorous photoprotection and surveillance with early excision.
pitfalls: Dismissing the macular lesions as ordinary pityriasis versicolor
Failing to distinguish inherited EV from an acquired EV-like phenotype that signals underlying immunodeficiency
Under-appreciating the malignant potential and neglecting long-term skin surveillance
Pursuing aggressive destruction of all warts rather than targeted management with cancer surveillance
management: Enforce strict lifelong photoprotection with sun avoidance, broad-spectrum sunscreen and protective clothing, as this is the central measure to limit ultraviolet-driven malignant transformation
Treat wart-like and dysplastic lesions with topical retinoids, imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil or cryotherapy, and use systemic retinoids (acitretin) for widespread or refractory disease
Undertake regular total-body skin surveillance with dermoscopy and biopsy any changing, indurated or ulcerated lesion
Excise cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas early, using margin-controlled (Mohs) or wide surgical excision for aggressive tumours
In acquired EV-like disease, screen for and treat the underlying immunodeficiency, including HIV and GATA2 defects, and minimise iatrogenic immunosuppression where feasible
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive TMC6/TMC8 inheritance and arrange family testing
Refer to dermatology and clinical genetics for long-term coordinated care
